This page is written according to the US SOC/O*NET 45-3031.00 'Fishing and Hunting Workers' (the fixed index gives this asset the Chinese name whose English rendering is 'Fishing and hunting workers'; the former 45-3011.00 'Fishers and Related Fishing Workers' has been discontinued and merged into this occupation).

Verify with one paper exercise (entirely fictional, containing no real boat positions, fishing grounds or operating parameters): you are given a work task pack (target species and waters or forest area, available boats or vehicles and fishing gear or traps and navigation and communication equipment, weather and sea state or ground condition forecasts, permits and quotas and legal size rules, crew on board and shifts and safety equipment, expected landing or knock-off time, and one equipment failure or sudden weather change or crew injury situation). The task is to set the shift priorities, explain how departure or hunting preparation, setting and operating gear or traps, harvesting catch and sorting and measuring, on-board processing and preservation, and landing and unloading and handover link together, and write out the checklists needed, the safety and review points, the record and handover formats, and the actions that must be stopped and reported when beyond your own authority or safety conditions.

Signals worth considering more: willingness to work outdoors and on the water or in the field over the long term, the ability to cope with irregular hours and a work rhythm far from land, the ability to keep judgement under weather and equipment and personnel risk, and willingness to work per permit and quota and safety rules. Signals requiring caution: not being comfortable in water or being prone to seasickness, difficulty coping with physical load and long periods offshore or in the field, and imagining this work as being only about catch volume without regard for safety and regulations. Use the paper exercise on this page for self-checking rather than drawing conclusions from personality labels.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute recruitment, a capability score, or maritime and safety and legal conclusions.

First judge whether you are willing to make water or field harvesting work a long-term career: it requires switching between physical load and work safety and permit compliance and catch handling, and taking on physical and safety and compliance responsibility; verify with the paper exercise on this page.

The work of this occupation revolves around the cycle of 'departure or hunting preparation and checks — setting and operating gear or traps — harvesting catch and sorting and measuring — on-board or on-site processing and preservation — landing and unloading and handover and sale — records and maintenance and after-action review': setting and operating gear or traps in the target waters or forest area, harvesting catch and sorting and measuring it, processing and preserving it on board or on site, landing and unloading and handing over, while maintaining engines and gear and complying with permits and quotas and safety rules.

US SOC/O*NET 45-3031.00 'Fishing and Hunting Workers': hunt, trap, catch or gather wild animals or aquatic animals and plants; may use nets, traps or other equipment; may haul catch onto a ship or other vessel (Hunt, trap, catch, or gather wild animals or aquatic animals and plants. May use nets, traps, or other equipment. May haul catch onto ship or other vessel). The former 45-3011.00 'Fishers and Related Fishing Workers' has been discontinued and merged into this occupation.

Work environment | mainly water or field work, with conditions varying by sea area or waters or forest area and season and weather.
Physical load | requires standing and carrying and hauling nets or traps and handling heavy loads for long periods.
Safety risk | faces drowning, hypothermia, mechanical and rope injuries and sudden weather changes.

Schedule and season | working hours often follow the fishing season or hunting season and tides and weather, far from land or base.

When the vessel is unseaworthy or overloaded or conditions are insufficient in severe weather, when lifesaving and firefighting and communication equipment is missing or has failed, when a person is injured or falls overboard or becomes hypothermic, when fishing permits or quotas or closed seasons or legal sizes are in doubt, when catch hygiene or traceability records are untruthful, or when the work exceeds your authority or training, stop the relevant action and report per the procedure of the vessel owner or master and the competent authority.

entries.answer: This page is written according to the US O*NET-SOC 45-3031.00 'Fishing and Hunting Workers' (the fixed index gives this asset the Chinese name whose English rendering is 'Fishing and hunting workers'; the former 45-3011.00 'Fishers and Related Fishing Workers' has been discontinued and merged into this occupation): hunt, trap, catch or gather wild animals or aquatic animals and plants; may use nets, traps or other equipment; may haul catch onto a ship or other vessel. Specific tasks include: driving boats and operating navigation instruments; removing catch from gear and measuring it to ensure compliance with legal sizes; directing fishing or hunting operations and supervising crew; interpreting weather and vessel conditions to determine the response; travelling to work areas on foot or by vehicle or boat or snowmobile or helicopter; setting and maintaining gear and traps and nets; maintaining engines and gear; washing decks; using fish finding equipment to locate schools of fish; processing catch and fur; transporting catch to processing plants; taking part in wildlife management and research; operating and maintaining drones to conduct aerial surveillance of work areas. Common reported job titles include Commercial Fisherman, Deckhand, Fisherman, Lobster Fisherman, Fur Trapper, Hunter, Trapper and Wildlife Control Operator.
entries.question: What do fishing and hunting workers mainly do?

entries.answer: The focus of responsibility and the outputs differ: this occupation's main outputs are catching or hunting or trapping or gathering wild animals and aquatic animals and plants and processing the catch or game; water transport occupations and sailors and ship fuelers output driving and maintaining transport vessels and carrying passengers and cargo or providing on-board support; agricultural workers and farm and ranch and aquaculture workers output growing and feeding and managing terrestrial or aquatic organisms; loggers output felling and transporting and initially processing timber; forest and conservation workers output silviculture and maintenance and patrol monitoring of forests and habitat (without catching or hunting work); slaughtering and meat cutting and seafood processing workers output cutting and packing in processing facilities. The gathering and processing of this occupation is limited to taking part in water or field work yourself.
entries.question: How is it different from water transport occupations, sailors, agricultural workers and loggers?

entries.answer: US O*NET-SOC 45-3031.00 'Fishing and Hunting Workers': interest code RC (Realistic and Conventional), in Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation needed, SVP below 6.0); the education survey is about 45% below high school, 30% high school or equivalent and 15% some college with no degree; the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists no formal educational credential and moderate-term on-the-job training. Employment, growth and openings use the BLS employment projections definition: 2025 employment of about 28,200 people, a decline of about 4% over 2025—2035, and about 3,300 average annual openings (all from replacement needs). On wages, the US Department of Labor and the BLS state clearly that OEWS does not provide wage estimates for 45-3031 because of data limitations (the wage column of the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook is marked unavailable, the most recent being a median annual wage of 28,530 US dollars in May 2017), so this page does not provide this occupation's wage, nor does it pass off the median wage of the 'agriculture, forestry and fishing occupational group' as such.

entries.answer: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation needed, SVP below 6.0). The work context shows: outdoors exposed to all weather every day 89%; working more than 40 hours a week 80%; face-to-face discussions every day 58%; decision freedom very high 60%; continuous contact with others 45%; work schedule seasonal (only during certain seasons of the year) 57%; wearing common protective or safety equipment every day 58%; exposure to minor burns or cuts or bites or stings every day 45%. The work environment varies with region and waters or land and the species sought, and work is often carried out under hazardous conditions that may cause injury or death.

entries.answer: A more accurate judgement is that weather and sea state lookups, navigation and positioning and fish finding, organising catch and quota and permit records, and equipment maintenance logs will be assisted by tools, and the occupation as a whole will mainly be enhanced; work safety judgement, saving lives, catch handling and regulatory declarations will still be borne by trained and qualified personnel. The ILO 2023 study shows that task exposure varies greatly across occupations, with clerical task exposure highest, while physical and on-site gathering and transport work is limited in overall replacement, and technical feasibility does not mean institutional adoption, so the conclusion is that the way information and equipment support is used will change, not that the occupation will be wholly replaced.

This page therefore does not provide wage percentiles or a median for this occupation, nor does it pass off the 'agriculture, forestry and fishing occupational group' 2025 median annual wage of 36,630 US dollars as this occupation's wage. Income in this occupation is often settled by catch share or piece rate and by voyage or season and after deducting costs such as fuel and gear and crew wages, and fluctuates widely.

Most positions also require water and field work capability and equipment operation and catch handling experience, and may require crew qualifications and vessel certificates and medical examination and lifesaving and firefighting and first aid and water safety training and fishing or hunting permits. entries.answer: In the United States, operating vessels or taking on navigational positions may require a merchant mariner credential issued by the US Coast Guard, fishing or hunting work requires the corresponding permits and quotas, and safety and hygiene and wildlife protection rules must be complied with; in mainland China, fishing work requires a fishing permit and compliance with closed seasons and quotas, vessel operation requires the corresponding crew qualifications, and catch handling must meet food safety and traceability requirements. These requirements vary by country and region and work type and must be verified against the competent authority's original text; this page does not provide maritime or legal advice, nor does it equate certification and training completion with being able to take on master or safety decisions or major work responsibility.

entries.answer: The main risks centre on working and navigating in severe weather or sea states, equipment and gear failure and rope and mechanical injuries, a person overboard or injured or hypothermic, violation of fishing or hunting permits and quotas and closed seasons and legal sizes, catch hygiene and traceability and wildlife protection, and unclear handover and declaration with the vessel owner or buyers or the competent authority. Boundaries: vessel seaworthiness and navigation decisions, rescue and abandoning ship and accident reporting, determination of permits and quotas and closed seasons and legal sizes, and catch hygiene and traceability and wildlife disposition must be carried out by the master and vessel owner and the competent authority per law and procedure; this page only suggests directions to check.
